Russian Empire. A vast Eurasian autocracy that emerged in the seventeenth century and became one of the world's largest states, spanning eleven time zones from Eastern Europe to the Pacific Ocean. Beginning with the Romanov dynasty's establishment in sixteen thirteen under Michael Romanov, it grew through military conquest, imperial expansion, and bureaucratic centralization, reaching its greatest territorial extent by the nineteenth century. Under reforming monarchs like Peter One and Catherine Two, the empire modernized its military and administration, positioning itself as a major European power. The empire's internal contradictions—immense wealth alongside peasant serfdom, ambitious reforms amid rigid autocracy—eventually destabilized it, culminating in the nineteen seventeen Revolution and the Soviet Union's emergence.

The empire's foundations were laid after the Time of Troubles from fifteen ninety-eight to sixteen thirteen, a period of civil war and foreign intervention, when the Romanov family ascended the throne and restored stability. Tsar Michael Romanov from sixteen thirteen to sixteen forty-five established the Romanov dynasty and began the systematic incorporation of Siberia and the Far East through expeditions and military campaigns. The empire initially took the form of a tsardom, with the tsar claiming descent from Byzantine emperors and ruling with absolute authority sanctioned by Orthodox Christianity.

Peter One the Great from sixteen eighty-two to seventeen twenty-five modernized the military along European lines, built the navy, relocated the capital to Saint Petersburg on the Baltic, and fought the Great Northern War against Sweden to secure European access. Catherine Two the Great from seventeen sixty-two to seventeen ninety-six continued expansion, partitioning Poland with Prussia and Austria, conquering Ottoman territories, and patronizing the Enlightenment while maintaining absolute rule and serfdom. The empire defeated Napoleon in the Patriotic War of eighteen twelve, earning immense prestige and allowing Russia to emerge as a dominant European power at the Congress of Vienna.

Russia adopted a Table of Ranks system under Peter One, meritocratic in principle but serving the autocracy, creating a centralized bureaucracy and military hierarchy. Russian territory expanded dramatically through colonization and annexation: the Caucasus, Central Asia, Siberia, and eastern Poland came under imperial control by the nineteenth century. The nineteenth century saw a flourishing of Russian literature, music, and philosophy, with figures like Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, and Tchaikovsky creating works that rank among civilization's greatest achievements.

Alexander Two initiated the Great Reforms from the eighteen sixties to eighteen seventies, including the abolition of serfdom in eighteen sixty-one, judicial reform, and military modernization. Yet these reforms provoked both liberal demands for further change and conservative resistance. The empire's autocratic structure, combined with growing industrialization, created explosive social tensions. Radical revolutionaries, Marxists, and reform movements challenged tsarist authority throughout the nineteenth century. The Russo-Japanese War from nineteen hundred four to nineteen hundred five exposed military weakness, sparking the nineteen hundred five Revolution and forcing limited constitutional reforms, though the tsar retained ultimate power.

World War One placed catastrophic strain on the empire. Millions died in combat. The economy collapsed. Revolutionary sentiment intensified among soldiers, workers, and intellectuals. The February Revolution of nineteen seventeen overthrew Tsar Nicholas Two, ending the Romanov dynasty and imperial rule after three hundred four years, followed by the Bolshevik Revolution in October.

The Russian Empire stands as a paradox in history: a vast, culturally rich autocracy that produced some of humanity's greatest art and literature while maintaining one of the world's most rigid class systems and repressive political structures. Its expansion across Siberia and Central Asia reshaped world geography and geopolitics. Its defeats of Napoleon and triumph in the Napoleonic Wars established Russia as a great power capable of shaping European affairs. Yet the empire's fundamental contradiction—the coexistence of enlightened rulers and brutal serfdom, of artistic genius and political repression—made it inherently unstable. Its collapse in nineteen seventeen unleashed the Russian Revolution, which fundamentally transformed the twentieth century and created the Soviet Union, while its imperial legacy continues to shape Russian identity and territorial ambitions today. It connects to Peter One, the transformative tsar who modernized Russia and made it a European power, to Catherine Two, the enlightened despot who expanded the empire and patronized culture, to Alexander One, the tsar who defeated Napoleon and dominated the Congress of Vienna, to Nicholas One, the conservative tsar whose rigid autocracy resisted reform and liberal movements, to Alexander Two, the reform tsar who abolished serfdom and modernized the empire's institutions, to the Ottoman Empire, the rival power the Russians conquered territory from throughout the empire's history, to the Austro Hungarian Empire, the competing European power with whom Russia struggled for Balkan dominance, to the Romanov Dynasty, the royal family that ruled the empire for three centuries, and to the Russian Revolution, the overthrow of imperial rule that transformed Russia and the world.
